examples.better: What did you expect?
examples.note: A calm, curious question makes them explain the dig.

examples.flat: You're so articulate! (said with surprise)
examples.better: Thanks. I'd rather hear what you thought of the proposal.
examples.note: Redirects to the substance.

examples.flat: You look so much better than last time. You'd really let yourself go.
examples.better: I feel good, thanks. How's the garden?
examples.note: Takes the compliment, skips the dig, moves on.

examples.flat: I love that you don't care what people think of your clothes.
examples.better: I care what I think. And I love this jacket.
examples.note: Owns it with confidence.

examples.flat: You're actually smart, for once.
examples.better: That stung a little. I know you meant it as a joke, but can we drop the 'for once'?
examples.note: With someone close, name it kindly so it doesn't become a pattern.

examples.flat: Wow, you look good in this pic, way better than in person lol
examples.better: Ha. I'll take the first half.
examples.note: Light and unbothered, with no chasing.

mistakes: Laughing along, then stewing on it later.
Over-justifying ('I DO go to the gym').
Firing back an insult.
Ignoring a pattern from someone close to you.

drills.prompt: Respond to: 'You're braver than me, I could never wear that.'
models: Thanks, I love it.
It takes no bravery at all. Just good taste.

drills.prompt: On a date, they say: 'You're interesting. Not my usual type, though.'
models: Then this should be a fun experiment.
Good. Your usual type clearly wasn't working.

quiz.scenario: A colleague says: 'Good job, you finally got one right.' Best counter?
options: Thanks so much!
Well, you're not perfect either.
Thanks. What do you mean by 'finally'?
Say nothing and stew
quiz.why: A calm question accepts nothing and makes them own the dig.

quiz.scenario: Why do negs work on some people?
options: They're very funny
They make the target try to win approval to fix the small dig
They're honest feedback
They build trust
quiz.why: The tactic relies on unsettling confidence so the target chases; not chasing defuses it.

techniques.ethics: Teasing between people who like each other is play; a dig meant to lower someone's confidence so they'll chase you is manipulation.

techniques.name: Love Bombing
sources: Strutzenberg et al., Love-bombing: a narcissistic approach to relationship formation (2017)
techniques.summary: Notice when intense affection, gifts and future plans arrive faster than trust could, and set your own pace.
techniques.why: Flooding someone with early attention creates a feeling of debt and specialness that can make later control easier. Early research links love bombing with narcissistic traits and low self-esteem, though the evidence base is still small. The defence isn't suspicion of warmth; it's checking whether the pace respects your no.
steps: Notice the speed: 'soulmate' talk, big gifts, constant texts, big plans in week one.
Enjoy the warmth, but set your own pace.
State one small boundary and watch the reaction.
Judge them by how they handle your no, not by how big their yes is.

examples.flat: I've never felt this way. Let's go to Paris next month, I've already booked it.
examples.better: That's lovely, and it's too fast for me. Let's do dinner next week.
examples.note: Keeps the warmth, sets the pace, and tests their respect.

examples.flat: Good morning beautiful. Where are you? Why haven't you replied? I miss you so much.
examples.better: I like hearing from you. I'm busy in the day, so I'll reply in the evenings.
examples.note: A clear rhythm shows whether they can respect it.

examples.flat: You're my soulmate. I knew the moment I saw you.
examples.better: I like you too. I'd like to get to know you before I decide about souls.
examples.note: Light humour slows the story down.

examples.flat: You're the only one who really gets me. The others are so fake.
examples.better: I'm glad we're close. I like the others too.
examples.note: Gently refuses the isolation hook.

examples.flat: You're the best hire I've ever made, you're family. Now, about this weekend...
examples.better: Thank you. I can't work this weekend, but I'll be in early on Monday.
examples.note: Accepts the praise and separates it from the ask.

examples.flat: We love you guys, we'll be partners for decades, so just sign the exclusivity clause.
examples.better: We love the relationship too. Let's start with a one year term and grow from there.
examples.note: Warmth doesn't buy a long commitment.

examples.flat: I bought you a necklace. Can we just forget about last night?
examples.better: Thank you. I still need us to talk about last night.
examples.note: Gifts don't replace repair.

mistakes: Treating all generosity as a red flag.
Feeling you owe them because they gave so much.
Explaining your boundary over and over.
Ignoring anger when you slow things down; that reaction is the real signal.

drills.prompt: After two dates they say: 'I've told my parents all about you, they want to meet you this weekend!'
models: That's sweet. It's early for me to meet parents. Let's keep it just us for a while.
I'm flattered. Not yet. Let's get to know each other first.

drills.prompt: A new friend says: 'I bought us concert tickets, so you have to come, I've already paid!'
models: That's generous, and I can't make it. Could you sell them or take someone else?
Thank you, but please check with me before buying things for me.

quiz.scenario: What best separates love bombing from ordinary enthusiasm?
options: They text often
They react badly when you set a small boundary
They pay you compliments
They plan a nice date
quiz.why: Enthusiastic people adjust to your pace; love bombers push back when you slow down.

quiz.scenario: Two weeks in, they say: 'Let's move in together.' Best response?
options: Yes, why not?
Absolutely not, you're crazy.
Ignore it and change the subject
I love how much you like me. It's too soon for me. Let's keep dating and see.
quiz.why: Warm, clear and paced: you keep the good feeling and your judgement.

techniques.ethics: Enthusiasm is fine; flooding someone with affection to create debt or speed past their judgement is manipulation.

techniques.name: DARVO & Gaslighting
techniques.aka: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender; reality denial
sources: Freyd, Violations of power, adaptive blindness, and betrayal trauma theory (1997)
Harsey, Zurbriggen & Freyd, Perpetrator responses to victim confrontation (2017)
Harsey & Freyd, DARVO: what is the influence on perceived perpetrator and victim credibility? (2020)
techniques.summary: Recognise when a confrontation gets flipped so you end up apologising, or your memory gets questioned, and hold on to the original point.
techniques.why: DARVO, a pattern named by psychologist Jennifer Freyd, denies the issue, attacks the person raising it, then casts the offender as the victim. Studies link hearing it with more self-blame, and found that people who know about DARVO are less swayed by it. Gaslighting works by making you doubt your own perception, so notes and facts restore your footing.
steps: Write down what happened, soon after it happens.
Put your point in one sentence and keep returning to it.
Acknowledge their feelings without dropping your point.
State your memory once; don't debate it.
If it's a pattern, get outside support from someone you trust.

examples.flat: That never happened. You're always imagining things. Honestly, I'm the one who should be upset.
examples.better: I remember it clearly, and I'm not going to argue about my memory. I'm upset about what you said on Friday.
examples.note: States reality once and returns to the issue.

examples.flat: I never agreed to that deadline. Why are you attacking me in front of everyone?
examples.better: I'm not attacking you. Here's the email from the 3rd. Let's sort out the deadline.
examples.note: Facts and calm undercut the reversal.

examples.flat: Wow, after everything I've been through, you bring THIS up?
examples.better: I know you've had a hard time, and I care. I still need to talk about the money.
examples.note: Holds compassion and the point together.

examples.flat: You're too sensitive, it was a joke. Now you've ruined dinner.
examples.better: It may have been a joke to you. It hurt me. Saying so isn't ruining dinner.
examples.note: Rejects the reversal without escalating.

examples.flat: You're crazy. I never said I was single.
examples.better: You did, last Tuesday, and I have the messages. I'm done here.
examples.note: Short, factual, and you leave.

examples.flat: We never promised delivery by June, and frankly your accusation is insulting.
examples.better: Clause 4.2 says June. I'm not accusing you, I'm asking what you'll do about it.
examples.note: Points to the record and the request.

examples.flat: Stop twisting my words. You always make me the bad guy.
examples.better: I'm not trying to make you the bad guy. The comment upset me. Can we talk in person?
examples.note: Lowers the heat while keeping the point.

mistakes: Arguing every detail, so you lose the thread.
Apologising for raising the issue at all.
Doubting yourself without checking your notes.
Handling a repeated pattern alone instead of talking to someone you trust.

drills.prompt: Respond to: 'I can't believe you'd accuse me of that after all I do for you. You're the one with the problem.'
models: I'm not saying you're a bad person. What happened on Saturday hurt, and I want to talk about it.
I hear that you're hurt. My point still stands: the comment at the party wasn't ok.

drills.prompt: A colleague says: 'I never said you could take the lead. You're making things up again.'
models: We talked about it on the 12th and I sent a recap afterwards. Let's look at it together.
I have the recap email. If you've changed your mind, that's fine, let's talk about that instead.

quiz.scenario: What does DARVO stand for?
options: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender
Defend, Agree, Resolve, Verify, Overcome
Doubt, Argue, Repeat, Validate, Object
Distract, Accuse, Retreat, Vent, Obey
quiz.why: Knowing the pattern by name makes it easier to spot, and research suggests it reduces its pull.

quiz.scenario: You raise a concern and they say: 'You're crazy, that never happened, and I'm hurt you'd even say it.' Best move?
options: Apologise for upsetting them
Spend an hour proving your memory
State your memory once, acknowledge their feelings, and return to your concern
Keep shouting until they admit it
quiz.why: You stay anchored to the issue without getting pulled into a fight about reality.

techniques.ethics: Disagreeing about what happened is normal; denying someone's reality and flipping the blame to escape accountability is manipulation.

techniques.name: Pressure Past a No
techniques.aka: Foot-in-the-door abuse, the low-ball, wearing you down
sources: Freedman & Fraser, Compliance without pressure: the foot-in-the-door technique (1966)
Cialdini et al., Low-ball procedure for producing compliance (1978)
techniques.summary: Spot when small yeses are being stacked into a big one, or a no is treated as an opening bid, and make your no stick.
techniques.why: Agreeing to a small request makes us more likely to agree to a bigger one, because we like to act consistently with what we've already done. Pressure tactics also use fatigue: they keep asking until refusing feels harder than giving in. Seeing the pattern lets you judge each ask on its own.
steps: Judge each request fresh: would I say yes if this were the first ask?
Say no once, briefly, without a reason they can argue with.
Repeat the same words calmly if they push.
End the conversation or leave if they keep going.

examples.flat: Come on, one more drink. Ok, just come up for a coffee. Just ten minutes.
examples.better: I've had a lovely time and I'm heading home. Goodnight.
examples.note: Clear and warm, with no gap to negotiate.

examples.flat: Since you've chosen the base model, you'll want the warranty, and the service plan, and...
examples.better: I agreed to the base model. That's what I'm buying.
examples.note: Separates the first yes from the add-ons.

examples.flat: You made the slides, so you might as well present them. And take the questions. And the follow-up.
examples.better: Happy with the slides. Presenting is a separate job, and I can't take it this week.
examples.note: Judges each ask on its own.

examples.flat: You said maybe! Maybe means yes, come on!
examples.better: Maybe meant I'd think about it. I've thought about it. No.
examples.note: Turns a maybe into a clean no.

examples.flat: Just sign here, it's only a formality, then we'll talk about the house.
examples.better: I don't sign anything I haven't read. Send it over and I'll get back to you.
examples.note: Refuses the small step toward a big commitment.

examples.flat: Why not? Give me one good reason.
examples.better: I don't need a good reason, I just don't want to. Let's pick something else.
examples.note: A no doesn't have to win a debate.

examples.flat: Pleeease. You owe me. Just this once.
examples.better: I've answered. Still no. Talk tomorrow.
examples.note: Repeats, closes, moves on.

mistakes: Giving reasons that invite counter-arguments.
Softening the no into a maybe.
Feeling you must stay consistent with an earlier yes.
Staying in the conversation long after the no.

quiz.scenario: Why does a small yes make a bigger yes more likely?
options: Small requests are always fair
People like to act consistently with what they've already agreed to
Big requests are more exciting
It's random
quiz.why: The consistency pull is what foot-in-the-door tactics exploit; judging each ask fresh breaks it.

quiz.scenario: Someone says: 'Why not? Give me one reason.' Best response?
options: List all your reasons
Agree to avoid conflict
Make up an excuse
I don't need a reason. No, thanks.
quiz.why: Reasons give them something to argue with; a calm no without one closes the door.

techniques.ethics: Asking again later is normal; treating a no as an obstacle to wear down is coercion.
